slides.title: Chapter 9: Transaction Fees
slides.sub: Who pays a fee, how it is priced, replaced and bumped, and what moved since print

items.body: Python 3.14.6 on the chapter's own library; Bitcoin Core 31.1 results are recorded from one test run, not run here.

slides.notes: This deck explains transaction fees: who pays them, how they are priced, how a payment is replaced or bumped, and what changed since the book went to print. Every number on a result picture was computed with the chapter's own Python library. Bitcoin Core 31.1 was run once on a test network, and its answers are only read back.

slides.title: Today's route
slides.sub: Seven parts; every number is a slide you can jump to

items.label: code examples with a picture of each result

slides.notes: The route has seven parts that follow the order of the chapter. Four true stories and twenty-seven code examples are spread across them. The examples are listed in the same order in the chapter code tab of the course page, so every listing here can be run and edited there.
slides.take: Seven parts, twenty-seven examples, four true stories

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers
slides.sub: Each has an answer on a slide; we return to them in the summary

items: Who pays a transaction fee, and why is it not a field of the transaction?
How is a fee rate computed, and which minimum rates apply?
How does a node estimate a fee, and what do two real blocks show?
What must a replacement pay, and why is full replacement now the default?
How does a child pay for its parent, and what does package relay add?
How can a family pin a payment, and what do TRUC and anchors change?
What is fee sniping, and why do wallets lock a payment to the tip?

slides.notes: The seven questions are the chapter's own, rewritten so that each has an answer on a slide. We return to them in the summary. A reader who can answer all seven has understood the chapter.

slides.title: One chapter, seven parts
slides.sub: The concept map the whole deck hangs on
slides.notes: The chapter has seven parts and 31 key concepts. Each part gets a divider, concept cards with everyday comparisons, code that runs, and some parts a true story. The deck follows the order of the chapter.
slides.take: Seven parts; every slide today lives on this map

slides.title: Who pays the fee
slides.sub: The spender pays the fee, like a tip left on the counter.

items.meaning: The fee is inputs minus outputs; no field holds it.
items.analogy: Think of the change you forget to take back from the counter.

items.meaning: Only the spender can add to the fee, since the signature covers the amounts.
items.analogy: Think of a cheque that cannot be altered after it is signed.

items.meaning: Miners choose what goes into a block and prefer the highest rates.
items.analogy: Think of a bus driver who boards the highest bidders first.

slides.notes: A transaction has no fee field. The fee is what the inputs hold and the outputs do not claim, so the spender pays it and only the spender can change it. This part shows how to see that, and what goes wrong when change is forgotten.

slides.title: A fee is a difference, not a field
slides.sub: Parsing a real transaction from its raw bytes

groups.note: An independent parser reads the raw bytes of one transaction.
It finds inputs, outputs and a lock time, but no fee field.

rows: outs = sum(o['value'] for o in t['vout'])
groups.note: The fee is what is left: inputs minus outputs.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: what the parser finds

rows: Fee field in the parsed payment

items.body: No field states the fee. It is the difference: 1,900,000,000 satoshis, left unclaimed by the outputs.

slides.notes: A transaction lists its inputs and its outputs, and nothing else. The miner's fee is whatever the inputs hold and the outputs do not claim. We parse the raw bytes ourselves and find 1,900,000,000 satoshis left over, with no field to name them. It is example 1 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Nothing in the transaction states the fee: it is inputs minus outputs

slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: inputs
items.meaning: Earlier outputs that a payment spends, each one entirely.
items.analogy: Think of banknotes from your wallet, handed over whole.

items.label: outputs
items.meaning: The new amounts, each with the lock that says who may spend it next.
items.analogy: Think of the sealed envelopes you fill for each recipient.

items.label: change output
items.meaning: An output that sends the rest of an input back to the spender.
items.analogy: Think of the coins a cashier hands back to you.

items.label: payments
items.meaning: Value moving from one holder to another, as a person sees it.
items.analogy: Think of passing a note across a table to a friend.

slides.notes: These cards cover inputs, outputs, change output and payments. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 9.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Forgetting the change
slides.sub: A 20 coin input, a 1 coin output and no change output

groups.note: A payment spends 20 coins, sends 1 and forgets its change.
The node's error text names the safety limit maxfeerate.
Mined with the limit lifted, the miner gets subsidy plus fee.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: the miner's reward, satoshis
The node said max-fee-exceeded. With the limit lifted, the reward 4,400,000,000 equals subsidy plus fee: yes.

slides.notes: If a wallet forgets the change output, the difference becomes a gigantic fee. The node refuses the payment with max-fee-exceeded. Mined with the limit lifted, the miner's reward equals the subsidy plus that fee, which shows where the money went. It is example 2 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: A safety limit protects the spender from paying nearly everything as fee

slides.title: Who pays the fee: key concepts (3 of 3)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: transactions
items.meaning: The signed records that spend inputs and create outputs.
items.analogy: Think of a cheque that lists the notes it uses and who gets what.

items.label: overpaying transaction fees
items.meaning: A fee far above what the market needs, wasted on the miner.
items.analogy: Think of paying for express delivery on an empty street.

items.label: excessive fees
items.meaning: A fee so high that a node refuses it unless told otherwise.
items.analogy: Think of a till that rejects a price with a zero too many.

items.label: absurd fees
items.meaning: A fee above the safety limit, usually a forgotten change output.
items.analogy: Think of a bank that asks twice before wiring a million.

slides.notes: These cards cover transactions, overpaying transaction fees, excessive fees and absurd fees. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 9.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Only the spender can raise the fee
slides.sub: Editing an amount after signing

groups.note: One payment as signed, and a copy with its output cut.
The node rejects the copy: the signature covers the amounts.
The cut is the extra fee; only the spender could add it.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: the same payment, signed and edited
The cut of 5,000 satoshis breaks the signature: mempool-script-verify-flag-failed.

slides.notes: We cut the first output of a signed payment by 5,000 satoshis. The node rejects the copy because the signature no longer fits. So the fee belongs to the spender; anyone else must pay in a second transaction, which is the idea of child pays for parent. It is example 3 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: The signature covers the amounts, so nobody else can add to the fee

slides.title: Fees and fee rates
slides.sub: A fee is a bill, and the rate is its price per unit of space.

items.meaning: Virtual size is the space a payment takes in a block.
items.analogy: Think of postage priced by the volume of the parcel.

items.meaning: A rate is the fee over the virtual size, in satoshis per byte.
items.analogy: Think of the price per kilo on a market scale.

items.meaning: Nodes, wallets and dust rules each set a floor.
items.analogy: Think of a minimum fare below which no taxi starts the meter.

slides.notes: Miners are paid by the space a payment takes, not by its value. This part measures size, weight and virtual size, turns a fee into a rate, and meets the floors that nodes, wallets and dust rules set.

slides.title: Fees and fee rates: key concepts
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Fees and Fee Rates
items.meaning: A fee is a sum in satoshis; a rate divides it by size.
items.analogy: Think of a freight bill: the total, and the price per cubic metre.

items.label: fee rates
items.meaning: The price per virtual byte by which miners sort payments.
items.analogy: Think of the price per kilo at a market stall.

items.label: blocks
items.meaning: Batches of payments, limited to four million units of weight.
items.analogy: Think of a bus that leaves every ten minutes with fixed seats.

slides.notes: These cards cover Fees and Fee Rates, fee rates and blocks. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 9.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Size, weight and virtual size
slides.sub: Three measures of one payment

groups.note: One payment of the test node, parsed from its hex text.
Witness bytes count a quarter, so weight is not size.
Virtual size is weight over four, rounded up.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: four measures of one payment
Virtual size 141 is the weight 561 over four, rounded up: the ratio is 0.2513.

slides.notes: One payment has 113 bytes without witness data and 222 bytes in all. Its weight is 561 units, because witness bytes count one each and the other bytes four. Its virtual size is 141, the weight over four rounded up. Fees and block space use this unit.
slides.take: Fees are charged per virtual byte, which is the weight over four

slides.title: A fee rate and its units
slides.sub: Satoshis per virtual byte, or coins per thousand bytes

groups.note: The rate is the fee divided by the virtual size.
Coins per thousand bytes convert to satoshis per byte.
Two spellings of one rate give one fee: mind the units.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: rates and their units
A coin-per-kilobyte rate is a hundred thousand times smaller as a number than the same rate in satoshis per byte.

slides.notes: The rate is the fee over the virtual size: 282 over 141 gives 2 satoshis per byte. Some tools speak in coins per thousand bytes, so 0.0000657 means 6.57 satoshis per byte. Two spellings of ten satoshis per byte give the same fee, and a wrong factor gives an absurd one.
slides.take: Mixing the units changes the fee by a factor of a hundred thousand

slides.title: Space in a block is limited
slides.sub: The block weight limit and a real block

groups.note: The limit is a consensus constant in the saved source.
Block 840,000 weighs almost exactly as much as the limit.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: weight units of a block
The block fills 99.83 percent of the 4,000,000 units, so payments compete for room.

slides.notes: The consensus limit is four million units of weight per block. Block 840,000 weighs 3,993,281, which is 99.83 percent of it. When blocks are full, payments must bid for room, and the fee rate is the bid. It is example 6 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: A full block makes fee rates compete

slides.title: The minimum relay fee
slides.sub: Why 14 satoshis were not enough for 141 bytes

groups.note: Three payments of 141 bytes, paying 8, 14 and 15 satoshis.
Only the last is taken; the node's floor is 0.1 per byte.
141 bytes at that floor cost 14.1, so 15 is the least.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: three fees for 141 virtual bytes
At 0.1 satoshi per byte, 141 bytes cost 14.1 satoshis: 15 is the smallest whole fee.

slides.notes: A node relays only payments above its floor, here a tenth of a satoshi per byte. For 141 bytes that is 14.1 satoshis, so 8 and 14 are refused and 15 is accepted. The floor protects nodes from spam, and it is policy, not consensus. It is example 7 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: A fee below the floor is not relayed, however valid the payment

slides.title: Dust and the wallet's floor
slides.sub: Outputs too small to be worth spending

rows: wal = ['ok' in w[k] for k in ks]
groups.note: The wallet refuses 0.5 and 0.1 satoshis per byte, takes 1.

rows: dust = {k: (n + 67) * 3 for k, n in sz.items()}
groups.note: Dust costs more to spend than it holds: (size + 67) x 3.
The limits in satoshis; the anchor output is smallest.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: dust limit of three output types, satoshis
The wallet refused 0.5 and 0.1 satoshis per byte and took 1: refused, refused, accepted.

slides.notes: An output is dust when spending it would cost more than it holds. The limit is three satoshis for each byte of the output plus its spending input, 294 for the common segwit key. The wallet in this run also refuses rates below one satoshi per byte. It is example 8 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Wallets keep stricter floors than nodes; dust is a floor on outputs

slides.title: Fee estimation
slides.sub: Estimating a fee is guessing the fare from past journeys.

items.meaning: The estimator reads recent blocks to answer for a target.
items.analogy: Think of a driver who recalls the usual fare for each hour.

items.meaning: Two real blocks show how far fee rates can move.
items.analogy: Think of seat prices at the rush hour and at midnight.

slides.notes: A wallet must guess a rate that will confirm in time. We see how the estimator learns from blocks, where its answers stop, and how two real blocks show a market that moves by a factor of five hundred.

slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.analogy: Think of a taxi driver who knows the usual fare for each hour.

items.label: Bitcoin Core
items.meaning: The reference node software whose rules and estimator the chapter measures.
items.analogy: Think of the reference clock by which other clocks are set.

slides.title: An estimate needs history
slides.sub: A new node cannot yet say what a fee should be

groups.note: A node with no blocks answers an estimate with an error.
After 120 rounds of test traffic it has history to use.
Estimates for targets of 2, 6 and 25 blocks, in sat per byte.

Before: 'Insufficient data or no feerate found'. After 120 rounds the estimate is about 1.2 satoshis per byte at every target.

slides.sub: A target of 144 blocks answered with 60

The default mode gives the economical answer at every target.
The cautious conservative mode differs at 144 blocks.

slides.title: Two blocks, two fee markets
slides.sub: The median fee rate of the highest-paying payments

groups.note: The census holds the 599 best-paying payments of two blocks.
The median fee rate fell from over a thousand to three.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: median fee rate, sat per byte
Among the 599 highest-paying payments of each block, the median rate fell from 1,436.45 to 3.02.

slides.notes: The census holds the 599 highest-paying payments of the halving block 840,000 and of block 971,489. The median rate in the first was 1,436.45 satoshis per byte and in the second 3.02. A fee estimate is only as good as the market it was learned in. It is example 11 in the chapter code tab of the course page.

slides.title: Replace by fee (RBF)
slides.sub: Replacing a payment is raising your bid at an auction.

items.meaning: A sequence number says whether replacement is welcome.
items.analogy: Think of a sticker that says this seat may be swapped.

items.meaning: A new copy must pay more than the old one, by a step.
items.analogy: Think of an auction bid that must beat the last one by a step.

items.meaning: Replacements can pay a payee twice or be cycled to cause harm.
items.analogy: Think of a cheque cashed twice because two copies exist.

slides.notes: A payment that waits too long can be replaced by a copy that pays more. We run the signal, the rules a replacement must meet, the default that changed, and the hazards of replacing.

slides.title: Replace by fee (RBF): key concepts
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Replace By Fee (RBF) Fee Bumping
items.meaning: Send a conflicting copy that pays more, so miners prefer it. Also written: RBF (replace by fee) fee bumping.
items.analogy: Think of raising your bid at an auction by at least one step.

items.label: BIP 125 opt-in replaceability signal
items.meaning: An input sequence below 0xfffffffe marks a payment as replaceable.
items.analogy: Think of a sticker that says this seat may be swapped.

items.label: conflicting transactions
items.meaning: Two payments that spend the same output; only one can be mined.
items.analogy: Think of two cheques written against the same banknote.

items.label: fee bumping
items.meaning: Raising the fee of a waiting payment, by replacement or by a child.
items.analogy: Think of adding stamps to a letter that is stuck in the post.

slides.notes: These cards cover Replace By Fee (RBF) Fee Bumping, BIP 125 opt-in replaceability signal, conflicting transactions and fee bumping. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 9.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: The opt-in replacement signal
slides.sub: BIP 125: a sequence number that invites replacement

groups.note: A low enough input sequence number signals replaceability.
Most payments of the halving block signal; fewer later.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: the signal and its use
One low sequence number is enough to signal, and fewer payments signal in the later block.

slides.notes: A payment signals that it may be replaced when one of its inputs has a sequence number below 0xfffffffe. In the halving block 485 of 599 payments signalled; in block 971,489 only 273. The signal matters less now that replacement needs no signal. It is example 12 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Any input with a sequence below 0xfffffffe signals replaceability

slides.title: A replacement must pay enough
slides.sub: Four conflicting copies of one 564-satoshi payment

groups.note: A payment of 564 satoshis meets four conflicting copies.

rows: taken = ['ok' in X[k]['result'] for k in ks]
groups.note: Each copy has its own fee; the node accepts or refuses.
Rule: old fee plus new size at the incremental rate.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: four copies of a 564-satoshi payment
The old fee plus the new size at the incremental rate: 579 pass, 578 do not.

slides.notes: A replacement must pay more than the payment it replaces, and also pay for its own size at the incremental rate. For a payment of 564 satoshis and 141 bytes that is 579. The copies at 514, 564 and 578 are refused, and the one at 579 is accepted.
slides.take: Pay the old fee plus the new size at the incremental rate

slides.title: Full replacement is the default
slides.sub: A payment that never signalled is replaced

groups.note: The first payment has a final sequence: it never signalled.
Yet a conflicting payment replaced it: full replacement is on.
The switch to turn that off was removed in 29.0.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: a payment that never signalled
A payment without a signal was replaced, and the switch that turned this off is gone.

slides.notes: The first payment used the final sequence number, so it never asked to be replaceable. A conflicting payment replaced it anyway. Release 28.0 made full replacement the default and 29.0 removed the option, so starting the node with it off now fails. It is example 14 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Bitcoin Core 31.1 replaces without a signal and has no switch to stop it

slides.title: A node that only listens to replacements
slides.sub: Peter Todd's build, 12 December 2022

items.cap: Accepted Here sign - ninjarobot, CC0, Wikimedia Commons

items: WHAT: On 12 December 2022 Peter Todd posted a build of Bitcoin Core 24.0.1 that carries Antoine Riard's full-rbf peering code.
WHY: Release 24.0.1 had added the option mempoolfullrbf, off by default, so only payments that signalled could be replaced.
HOW: The build advertises a FULL_RBF service bit and connects to four more nodes that do the same, so replacements travel reliably.
SO WHAT: Bitcoin Core 28.0 made full replacement the default and 29.0 removed the option, as the previous slide ran.

items.body: Stand-in picture: an accepted-here sign, not the post

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 2022-12-12. On Monday 12 December 2022 Peter Todd posted to the bitcoin-dev list a build of Bitcoin Core 24.0.1 with Antoine Riard's full-rbf peering code. The lesson is that policy is what most nodes choose to relay, and it changes by their choice.

slides.sub: Three versions of one payment

groups.note: Three versions of one payment, each replacing the last.
Versions 0 and 1 conflict, 1 and 2 conflict, 0 and 2 do not.
So 0 and 2 can both be mined: the payee is paid twice.

items.body: Result: payee's amount, satoshis
Versions 0 and 2 do not conflict (no): both were mined and the payee got double.

slides.notes: Three versions of a payment replace each other in turn. Versions 0 and 2 do not conflict, so once version 0 is mined, version 2 can be mined too. The payee asked for 40,000,000 satoshis and received 80,000,000. The sender pays twice.
slides.take: Replacing is not undoing: an old version may still be mined

slides.title: Policy or consensus?
slides.sub: Why a payment can be valid and still not be relayed

left.head: Consensus decides what is valid
rows: Every node must agree, or the chain splits.
The block weight limit is one such rule.
A change needs a soft or hard fork.

right.head: Policy decides what is relayed
rows: Each node may choose its own rules.
Relay floor, replacement rules, TRUC and cluster limits are policy.
A change needs only a new release.

slides.notes: Most rules of this chapter are policy: the relay floor, the replacement rules, the version 3 limits and the cluster limits. A payment that breaks them can still be valid in a block that a miner builds. Policy changes with a release; consensus changes only by a fork.
slides.take: Policy can change with a release; consensus changes only by a fork

slides.title: Child pays for parent (CPFP)
slides.sub: A child pays for its parent, like a friend who covers your fare.

items.meaning: Miners price a parent and its child together.
items.analogy: Think of a shopper who buys the bundle with the best price per item.

items.meaning: Nodes accept a pair that a single payment could not be.
items.analogy: Think of a gate that admits a pair who pay the entry together.

items.meaning: Connected payments are grouped and ordered as one cluster.
items.analogy: Think of a timetable that sorts linked carriages together.

slides.notes: When the parent cannot be changed, a child can pay for it. We measure the package rate, see why nodes now relay packages, and meet the cluster mempool that replaced the old chain limits.

slides.title: Child pays for parent (CPFP): key concepts
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Child Pays for Parent (CPFP) Fee Bumping
items.meaning: A child spends the parent's output and pays enough for both. Also written: CPFP (child pays for parent) fee bumping.
items.analogy: Think of a friend who pays your fare together with his own.

items.label: Package Relay
items.meaning: Nodes judge a parent and its child together, not one by one.
items.analogy: Think of a gate that admits a pair when the pair pays the entry.

items.label: package fee rate
items.meaning: The pair's total fee over its total virtual size.
items.analogy: Think of the price per kilo of a parcel and its box together.

items.label: ancestor fee rate mining
items.meaning: Miners pick a payment with the ancestors it needs, by their joint rate.
items.analogy: Think of a shopper who buys the bundle because it is cheapest per item.

slides.notes: These cards cover Child Pays for Parent (CPFP) Fee Bumping, Package Relay, package fee rate and ancestor fee rate mining. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 9.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.sub: Child pays for parent, measured in a block

groups.note: A parent pays 141 satoshis, its child 14,100; 141 bytes each.
Alone, the parent pays 1 per byte and the child 100.
The miner prices the pair as one package.

The pair's 50.77 beats the waiting payment A at 20, so parent and child are mined together.

slides.sub: A child at 5 satoshis per byte

slides.title: Package relay
slides.sub: A parent below the floor, sent with its child

groups.note: A parent pays 8 satoshis; alone it misses the floor of 15.
Its child, sent first, fails: the parent is unknown.
As a package the pair is judged together and accepted.

items.body: Result: three ways to send the same pair
Alone, each fails; as a package the pair is judged by its combined rate.

slides.notes: A parent with 8 satoshis fails the relay floor of 15 on its own, and its child cannot be sent first because the parent is unknown. As a package the pair is judged by its combined rate and accepted. Limited package relay of one parent and one child exists since release 28.0.
slides.take: Nodes can judge a pair that a single payment would fail

slides.title: Cluster limits
slides.sub: The cluster mempool of Bitcoin Core 31

groups.note: The mempool groups connected payments into clusters with limits.
A chain of 65: 64 accepted, the next one refused.
The old 25-ancestor limit is gone: a chain of 26 passes.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: limits on one cluster
Size is limited per cluster; the old limit of 25 ancestors no longer applies.

slides.notes: Release 31.0 groups connected payments into clusters, limited to 64 payments and 101,000 virtual bytes. Of a chain of 65, 64 are accepted and the next is refused as a too-large cluster. The old limit of 25 ancestors is gone, so a chain of 26 is accepted. It is example 19 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Limits are set on clusters of connected payments, not on single chains

slides.title: Mempool size and expiry
slides.sub: Two defaults of the waiting room

groups.note: The defaults are constants in the saved Bitcoin Core source.
A waiting payment is dropped after 336 hours, which is 14 days.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: two defaults of the mempool
A payment may wait 14 days before the node forgets it.

slides.notes: The mempool holds 300 megabytes by default. A payment that waits too long is dropped after 336 hours, which is 14 days. The book speaks of about a day's worth, which describes neither default. It is example 20 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: A payment may wait fourteen days, not one

slides.title: Pinning and anchors
slides.sub: Pinning is a lorry parked behind your car; an anchor is a spare handle.

items.meaning: One extra small child was allowed beyond the usual limits.
items.analogy: Think of a lane kept free for the ambulance.

items.meaning: Version 3 payments get strict limits that bound pinning.
items.analogy: Think of a parking bay with a size limit for the car behind.

items.meaning: A small output lets any party add a fee later.
items.analogy: Think of a spare handle on a door.

slides.notes: A large child can make a parent costly to replace, and a pre-signed payment cannot guess a future fee. This part runs the carve-out, the TRUC limits and the pay-to-anchor output that answer both.

slides.title: Pinning and anchors: key concepts
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Transaction Pinning
items.meaning: A cheap parent made hard to replace by a big or crowded family.
items.analogy: Think of a lorry parked behind your car: the bigger it is, the dearer to move.

items.label: CPFP Carve Out and Anchor Outputs
items.meaning: Rules and outputs that keep a child possible when the fee is unknown in advance. Also written: carve outs (CPFP), anchor outputs (CPFP).
items.analogy: Think of a spare door handle that anyone can grab to add the fee later.

slides.notes: These cards cover Transaction Pinning and CPFP Carve Out and Anchor Outputs. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 9.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: A big child pins its parent
slides.sub: Replacing a parent costs more when its child is large

groups.note: A parent paying 705 satoshis gets a child of 90,012 bytes or 885.
To replace the parent, pay for the whole pinned family.
A capped version 3 child cuts the price about 88-fold.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: cost to replace the parent, satoshis
The parent pays 705. A pinned family of 90,012 bytes costs 450,780 to replace; a capped one only 5,145.

slides.notes: A parent that pays 705 satoshis gets a child of 90,012 bytes. To replace the parent, the replacer must pay for the whole family: 450,780 satoshis. With a version 3 child, capped at 1,000 bytes, the same replacement costs 5,145, about 88 times less. It is example 21 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Cap the size of the child and pinning becomes cheap to undo

slides.title: TRUC limits on a family
slides.sub: Version 3: one small child, and a better sibling replaces it

groups.note: A version 3 child may be 1,000 bytes at most; 1,350 fails.
A small child of 141 bytes is accepted without trouble.

rows: ev = ['sibling eviction' in r1, 'ok' in r2]
groups.note: A second child replaces the first only at a higher rate.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: limits of a version 3 family
The family stays small, and a better sibling can always replace a pinning one.

slides.notes: A version 3 parent may have one child of at most 1,000 virtual bytes. A child of 1,350 is refused and one of 141 is accepted. A second child at the same rate is refused, and one at a higher rate evicts its sibling, so a pin cannot last.
slides.take: Strict limits make the worst case of pinning small and known

slides.title: Pay to anchor
slides.sub: A zero-fee parent with an output anyone can spend

groups.note: A version 3 parent pays no fee and has one anchor output.
Alone it is refused; with its child it is accepted.
The child spends the anchor with an empty witness.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: the anchor and the package
The anchor carries no value and needs no key: the child that spends it brings the fee.

slides.notes: The parent has a zero-value output with the script 51024e73, which anyone can spend, and it pays no fee. Alone the node refuses it. The child spends the anchor with an empty witness and pays 10,000 satoshis, so the package is accepted. It is example 23 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: The parent pays nothing; the child brings the fee when it is needed

slides.title: The carve-out limit
slides.sub: What the book says and what the code says

groups.note: The extra descendant size is a constant in the Core source.
The book states another number; the saved text confirms it.

rows: gone = L.has(n, 'removed from the mempool logic')
groups.note: Release 31.0 removed the rule with the cluster mempool.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: three sources compared
The book and the code disagree by a factor of ten.

slides.notes: The carve-out allowed one extra child beyond the usual limits. The book gives its size as 1,000 virtual bytes, while the source code says 10,000. Release 31.0 removed the rule, because the cluster limits replaced the descendant limits it worked around. It is example 24 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Check the numbers of a book against the source code

slides.title: A pre-signed payment cannot guess its fee
slides.sub: Matt Corallo's proposal, 29 November 2018

items.cap: Lightning Network logo - Ole Henrik Skogstrom, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

items: WHAT: On 29 November 2018 Matt Corallo proposed that a Lightning commitment transaction may carry one extra small child.
WHY: Pre-signed transactions are broadcast much later, so their fee cannot be guessed and a child has to add it.
HOW: A counterparty could chain a large child of moderate rate to the output and pin the transaction; the carve-out allows one more small child.
SO WHAT: Release 0.19.0.1 shipped it with 10,000 bytes, not the 1,000 the book states, and 31.0 removed it.

items.body: Stand-in picture: the Lightning logo, not the proposal

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 2018-11-29. On Thursday 29 November 2018 Matt Corallo wrote that Lightning channels exchange pre-signed transactions that are broadcast much later, so their fee has to be predicted or added afterwards by a child. The lesson is that a limit built for one attack can outlive the problem it solved.

slides.title: Fee sniping and incentives
slides.sub: Fee sniping is a thief rewriting the last page of the ledger.

items.meaning: A block pays a subsidy and the fees of its payments.
items.analogy: Think of a wage plus tips whose mix changes over the years.

items.meaning: A miner may re-mine a block to take its best fees.
items.analogy: Think of a clerk who rewrites yesterday's entries to keep the big ones.

items.meaning: Wallets lock a payment to the next block height.
items.analogy: Think of dating a cheque so that it cannot be moved back.

slides.notes: A block pays a subsidy and fees, and the mix changes. When fees dominate, a miner may gain by re-mining a block. We compute the odds and see how wallets defend with the lock time.

slides.title: Fee sniping and incentives: key concepts
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Timelock Defense Against Fee Sniping
items.meaning: A wallet sets the lock time to the current height, so a rewritten block cannot take the payment.
items.analogy: Think of a ledger line dated today that cannot be moved to an older page.

items.label: fee sniping
items.meaning: A miner re-mines a block to take the payments with the best fees.
items.analogy: Think of a clerk who rewrites yesterday's entries to keep the big ones.

items.label: timelocks
items.meaning: Rules that make a payment valid only after a time or a height.
items.analogy: Think of a post-dated cheque.

items.label: lock time
items.meaning: The field of a transaction that holds that height or time.
items.analogy: Think of the date written on a post-dated cheque.

slides.notes: These cards cover Timelock Defense Against Fee Sniping, fee sniping, timelocks and lock time. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 9.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.sub: The reward of the halving block and of a later block

In the halving block the subsidy was only the remainder.

In the halving block the subsidy was 312,500,000 of 4,075,061,499 satoshis, the rest was fees.

slides.notes: In block 840,000 the fees were 3,762,561,499 satoshis of a 4,075,061,499 reward, so the subsidy of 312,500,000 was only the rest. That is 92.33 percent fees. In block 971,489 fees were 0.46 percent of the reward. It is example 25 in the chapter code tab of the course page.

slides.title: Block 840,000: fees were nearly the reward
slides.sub: ViaBTC and block 840,000, 20 April 2024

items.cap: Bitcoin mining farm - Marko Ahtisaari, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

items: WHAT: Block 840,000 was found on 20 April 2024 at 00:09 UTC by the pool ViaBTC and held 3,050 transactions.
WHY: It was the first block after the fourth halving, so the subsidy fell from 6.25 to 3.125 bitcoins.
HOW: Fees were 3,762,561,499 satoshis of a 4,075,061,499 reward, which is 92.33 percent; in block 971,489 they were 0.46 percent.
SO WHAT: The book says the subsidy is much higher than fees, which is true of the later block and false of this one.

items.body: Stand-in picture: a mining farm, not the pool ViaBTC

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 2024-04-20. Block 840,000 was found on 20 April 2024 at 00:09 UTC by the pool ViaBTC and held 3,050 transactions. The lesson is that check a book's claim against the block, because the market moves.

slides.title: Odds of winning a sniping race
slides.sub: How hash rate turns into the chance to re-mine a block

groups.note: The chance to win a re-mining race is (x/(1-x)) squared.

rows: pct = [round(100 * p, 2) for p in odds]
groups.note: At 45 percent two in three; at half the rate, certain.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: chance to win the re-mining race, percent
At 45 percent of the hash rate the chance is 66.94 percent; at half it is certain.

slides.notes: A miner with a share x of the hash rate wins the race to re-mine a block with probability x over one minus x, squared. That is 1.23 percent at 10 percent of the hash rate and 66.94 percent at 45. At half the hash rate the chance is certain.
slides.take: With 45 percent of the hash rate a miner wins two races in three

slides.title: What if nobody got a subsidy?
slides.sub: A Princeton paper, 21 October 2016

items.cap: Nassau Hall, Princeton University - Smallbones, CC0, Wikimedia Commons

items: WHAT: On 21 October 2016 Arvind Narayanan announced the paper On the Instability of Bitcoin Without the Block Reward on the Princeton CITP blog.
WHY: Rewards are expected to give way to fees, and when fees are the main income a miner can gain by undercutting a rival's block.
HOW: The chapter computes that a miner with 45 percent of the hash rate wins the race to re-mine a block with probability 66.94 percent.
SO WHAT: Fees must replace the subsidy, so the rules for fees must be stable; wallets defend with the lock time.

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 2016-10-21. On 21 October 2016 Arvind Narayanan announced on the Princeton CITP blog the paper On the Instability of Bitcoin Without the Block Reward, written with Miles Carlsten, Harry Kalodner and Matt Weinberg and presented at ACM CCS the next week.

rows: back = [g for g in gap if g]
groups.note: Most sit at the tip; a few are set back by some blocks.
A payment is not final in the block of its lock time.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L is the chapter library; R, R2 its runs

items.body: Result: lock times of 60 payments
A lock time at the tip keeps a payment out of any block that a sniper re-mines.

slides.notes: A wallet sets the lock time of a payment to the current height, so that a miner who rewrites the block cannot take it. Of 60 payments in the test, 56 sit at the tip and four are set back. Such a payment is not final in the block of that height.
slides.take: A lock time equal to the tip makes a re-mined block useless to the sniper

slides.title: The chapter in five lines
slides.sub: One line per group of parts, each provable from its slides

items: The fee is inputs minus outputs: no field holds it, and only the spender can change it.
Miners sort by fee rate in satoshis per virtual byte; the relay floor and dust set minimums.
A payment is replaced by a copy that pays the old fee plus its own size; full replacement is the default.
A child pays for its parent as one package; clusters, TRUC and anchors bound pinning.
When fees replace the subsidy, a miner may snipe a block, and wallets defend with the lock time.

slides.notes: These five lines are the deck in miniature. A line that feels unproven should send you back to its code slide, because every figure in it was computed there. The chapter code tab of the course page reruns all twenty-seven examples.
slides.take: If a line feels unproven, the code slide of its part carries the receipt
